newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN relief team to assess food needs in North Korea.
newsitem.headline: UN relief team to assess food needs in North Korea.

text.p: A United Nations team of experts is expected to evaluate emergency food needs in flood-hit North Korea later this month ahead of launching a new funding appeal, a U.N. spokeswoman said on Tuesday.
Madeleine Moulin-Acevedo, spokeswoman of the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA), said that officials from donor countries were also to be invited on the assessment mission.
North Korea, hit hard by massive floods in 1995 and 1996, admitted last week it had only half the grain needed to feed its 23 million people, reliant on the public distribution system.
An official from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) last week predicted a disaster by year-end if aid was not forthcoming to the communist country.
"There is an assessment mission which should be leaving shortly for North Korea," Moulin-Acevedo told a news briefing.
"In principle it should leave at the end of February," she later told Reuters. "This has to be confirmed."

The New York-based DHA is coordinating U.N. relief to North Korea, where floods two years in a row left half a million people homeless and ruined rice fields, factories and livestock. Acute food shortages and malnutrition have been reported.
The U.N. plans to launch an inter-agency appeal for the reclusive state in March or April, to follow on a previous July 1996 appeal for $43.6 million. Donors only funded half of it.

South Korea said last week that it would consider contributing aid to Pyongyang if an international group makes a formal appeal. The United States also sent a strong signal that it was willing to help with the food problem.
Agencies active in North Korea and expected to take part in the mission include DHA, the Rome-based World Food Programme, U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organisation.
UNICEF is currently feeding some 100,000 children under age five in flood-stricken areas of North Korea, a spokesman said.
The agency has also vaccinated nearly one million children against measles, he added.
"We are working on an idea with WFP on seed distribution," he said. "The government is beginning to allow people to grow their own food, whereas before it was all controlled."
The IFRC representative in North Korea, Ole Gronning of Denmark, last week predicted a human disaster by the end of the year if relief did not arrive in the communist country.
"We will have a human disaster at the end of the year if the food (aid) is not coming. (By) July...there will be no food in the country," he said in Beijing.
The Geneva-based IFRC says food rations across North Korea are down to less than a quarter of the level normally considered essential to maintain a healthy population.
North Korea was forecast to consume 5.5 million tonnes of grain in 1997, but Pyongyang feared a shortfall of 45 percent, or up to 2.5 million tonnes, according to Gronning.
Some two percent of farmland had been completely destroyed, covered with sand several metres deep, he added.
Pyongyang's arch-rival South Korea, with whom it is still formally at war, has been one of the 25 donor countries, with its Red Cross pledging 1,000 tonnes of wheat flour and 15,000 pairs of socks.
Seoul suspended food shipments to North Korea after accusing Pyongyang of landing 26 commandos from a submarine last September. All but two of the group died during a manhunt.
The aid resumed after North Korea apologised and South Korea returned the remains of the infiltrators.
